transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-15
Start time: 14:30 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Riley Chen (Redwood SE), Alyssa Morgan (CTO, VectorScale), Diego Ramos (ML Eng), Priya Nair (Product), Samir Gupta (Infra)

Summary (auto-generated, may be rough): quick discovery to understand VectorScale's model selection constraints - context length needs, multilingual support, tool/function-calling, and deployment mode (hosted vs dedicated vs private). Customer wants benchmark + security docs.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. i'm jordan from redwood, i'll be the AE on the account, and riley is our se, riley do you want to intro?
[00:12] Riley: yeah hi all, riley chen, se - i work on model selection, perf, and private deployments. we'll mostly ask about your workloads, latency SLAs, and any constraints.
[00:20] Alyssa: thanks, yeah alyssa here. quick context - VectorScale builds inference for robotics control and multimodal planning, so low latency for short prompts is important but we also have some long-context planning for mission logs.
[00:33] Diego: hi, diego - our models ingest telemetry + operator notes, sometimes in english/spanish, and occasionally japanese. we need correct multilingual reasoning and tool calls to our internal task manager.
[00:45] Jordan: perfect; wanted to start with the big question - hosted vs dedicated vs private. what's your priority: speed to prod, isolation, or cost?
[00:54] Priya: product timeline is tight, speed to prod is high on the list but we also have enterprise customers who insist on data residency and KMS controls, so that pushes dedicated or private for certain tiers.
[01:08] Samir: infra wise, we prefer VPC peering for control plane, and on-prem for especially sensitive workloads. curious which redwood options match that.
[01:18] Riley: all right; quick mapping: hosted is fastest for onboarding, predictable cost per token but multi-tenant; dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools and network isolation; private gives you a managed control plane in your VPC or full on-prem. we can support KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs in private.
[01:34] Alyssa: good. second area: model families. we're evaluating open models - we've tried LLaMA-2 style variants, Mistral, MPT, and some of the larger open 70B+ ones. we need guidance on tradeoffs for accuracy vs latency/cost.
[01:48] Riley: okay, typical tradeoffs: model size and architecture determine latency and token cost, approx throughput. for short-turn responses (under 512 tokens) a 13B quantized model with optimized kernels often hits better latency/cost than a 70B that might be better for reasoning but is more expensive. for long-context runs we can recommend models with chunked attention or extended context architectures.
[02:12] Diego: our planning logs sometimes go to 50k tokens - we heard about 32k and 100k models. what's redwood's support for >32k contexts? any model you run that supports 100k?
[02:24] Riley: we do support extended contexts. there are a couple of open models with native 64k or 128k support, and we also do sliding-window + KV cache techniques to emulate longer contexts for some models. there is a cost and latency tradeoff - large context increases memory and can impact throughput. we can run a benchmark with your payload to see the real numbers.
[02:43] Jordan: we should note that some model names might be transcribed wrong in the notes - feel free to correct us offline.
[02:49] Alyssa: noted. third question: multilingual quality - we need consistent Spanish and Japanese performance, not just translation. any recommended models?
[02:58] Riley: Mistral-like and some Llama-derivatives perform well, but you may want mixes: an instruction-tuned multilingual model or a fine-tuned variant trained on your domain. we can run evals on your Spanish/Japanese prompt set as part of the benchmark.
[03:13] Diego: also we need tool-calling to our task manager (REST endpoints + internal RPC). is function-calling supported?
[03:19] Riley: yes - we support tool/function calling in the hosted api and in private deployments. for dedicated/private you can enforce network egress controls so tool calls can happen securely inside your VPC. there are example patterns for synching the KV cache and passing structured outputs.
[03:33] Priya: are there any limitations on streaming + function-calling combos? we do both streaming tokens to the operator UI and also want ordered function call invocations.
[03:41] Riley: streaming with function-calling is supported; our SDK provides event hooks so you can capture the call and the streaming tokens. edge cases exist - large functions that return big payloads can push memory. we'll detail in docs.
[03:54] Jordan: diving into performance - what's a realistic p99 latency for a 13B vs 70B on dedicated GPUs?
[04:02] Riley: ballpark: for optimized 13B quantized on A100 or similar you might see p95 around 150-300ms for short prompts (under 256 tokens). for 70B it can be 400ms-1s depending on quantization and kernel support. those are appx - your prompts and beam/temperature settings matter.
[04:22] Samir: and cost delta? we run many small queries per second, so per-token cost compounds.
[04:28] Riley: correct. smaller models with batching typically reduce unit cost; we can show a cost/per-token matrix once we see RPS and token distribution.
[04:38] Alyssa: security: SOC2, SAML/SSO for console, RBAC, and audit logs are must-haves. do you have any customers running private with HSM KMS?
[04:50] Jordan: yes, a few enterprise customers run private with customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations; we provide audit logs and can support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning. we'll share our security whitepaper.
[05:03] Diego: what about data retention and test datasets? we need to ensure training data can't be reconstructed - also some legal teams want to be sure that hosted logs aren't used to fine-tune models.
[05:14] Riley: by default hosted doesn't use customer data to retrain open models; we have options to disable telemetry ingestion and to configure retention. private gives you full control. we'll include that in the security docs.
[05:25] Priya: great. timeline - we want a pilot early q1, but we need benchmarks + security signoff first.
[05:33] Jordan: sounds doable; we'll run a benchmark within 1-2 weeks if you can provide sample prompts and a representative traffic pattern.
[05:40] Alyssa: note - our traffic has spikes at mission start times, occasionally up to 200 RPS for short bursts. average is ~20 rps.
[05:50] Riley: that's helpful. for bursty workloads we can recommend dedicated reserved capacity with burst buckets. alternatively, a hosted plan with autoscaling might be cheaper but less predictable for latency.
[06:03] Diego: curious about quantization and accuracy loss - do you recommend 4-bit for production?
[06:09] Riley: 4-bit quantization is common; for many instruction tasks it performs well but can slightly degrade some generation quality. we can test both 4-bit and int8/16b profiles during benchmarks. Redwood Optimize will also suggest quantization per workload.
[06:23] Priya: about model switching - can we start hosted with smaller models and then move to dedicated/private without changing code?
[06:29] Jordan: yes - one of our differentiators is a consistent API across hosted, dedicated, and private. you can pin model versions and routing policies. code change should be minimal - mostly config.
[06:40] Alyssa: good. Diego: for tool-calls, we need signed JWTs on the request to our task manager. any built-in support for mTLS or signed tokens?
[06:50] Riley: we support mTLS in private and dedicated networking setups; hosted can do secure function proxies and you can validate JWTs at your service.
[06:58] [07:00] Jordan: quick clarifying question - can you describe a sample user flow where the model needs 50k tokens? do you chunk or keep full context?
[07:10] Diego: the planning flow: telemetry stream + operator logs for last 48 hours, variable length, sometimes 30-50k tokens; then the model synthesizes a plan and issues actions to tools. we need coherent chain-of-thought across the long context.
[07:24] Riley: for that, we recommend either a model with native long context or a hybrid approach where only windowed context plus indexed retrieval is included. we also offer prefix caching so you don't resend static sections every time.
[07:36] Priya: will that affect latency dramatically?
[07:40] Riley: yes it can. long context increases memory and prefill time - we often see higher tail latencies. but for batched offline planning it's fine; for real-time control you'd want to keep critical context small and offload larger history to retrieval.
[07:54] Alyssa: this is leaning us toward a mixed architecture - small low-latency models for real-time control and larger models for offline planning in private. does redwood support routing across models by policy?
[08:04] Jordan: yes - smart routing can direct requests by latency or cost policy, fall back to smaller models on congestion, and you can pin routes per customer tier.
[08:14] Diego: one more - how do you handle KV cache invalidation across model versions during rollouts? we've seen cache staleness break completions.
[08:22] Riley: we expose cache flush controls and versioned KV keys. during rollouts you can use canary traffic and keep separate cache namespaces; we recommend orchestrated rollouts with automatic fallback. we'll share a rollout playbook.
[08:36] Jordan: switching to the benchmark ask - what we'll need from you: sample prompt set (multilingual), an RPS profile, and a few payload examples including tool call shapes. does that sound right?
[08:46] Alyssa: yes - i'll assign diego to collect a 200 prompt sample in english/spanish/japanese + 2 tool-call examples. also we'll provide a spec for 50k token planning example.
[08:56] Priya: legal will need the security docs before pilot - soc2/kms/retention example.
[09:02] Jordan: we'll send the security whitepaper and a baseline sso/se options doc.
[09:08] [09:10] Riley: quick note on model names - we recommend testing 13B quantized, a 30-40B mid-size for reasoning, and optionally a 70B for high-recall tasks. for multilingual, test an instruction-tuned multilingual 13-30b and a domain fine-tuned variant.
[09:27] Diego: on tool-calling latency - what's the expected round-trip for a function call that queries our internal DB?
[09:33] Riley: depends on your function latency; from the model layer we add minimal overhead (~10-30ms) for the call orchestration, but your function's response time dominates. in private with vpc peering and low network hops it's negligible.
[09:47] Alyssa: any recommended logging patterns to keep PII out of logs?
[09:52] Riley: yes - you can configure token masking and structured logging to avoid recording sensitive fields. we'll include patterns in the security doc.
[10:02] Jordan: okay - i'll recap the next steps at the end. moving on - pricing model question: do you price per-token on hosted and flat commit for dedicated?
[10:11] Riley: hosted is usage-based per token + optional minute/throughput charges for streaming; dedicated is reserved capacity with a monthly commit and potential overage rates; private is licensing + infra. we'll provide a pricing matrix.
[10:23] Priya: when you say reserved capacity, how fast can we scale up for unexpected spikes?
[10:29] Riley: dedicated has burst capacity options with autoscaling policies; for extreme spikes we offer overflow to hosted but that can have higher latency - we can configure automatic fallback.
[10:40] Diego: for the benchmark, can you include both quality metrics and cost per 1M tokens?
[10:44] Riley: yes we'll include latency p50/p95/p99, token cost estimates, and quality evals on your prompt set (BLEU/ROUGE/qual evals as applicable).
[10:56] [11:00] Jordan: small digression - any regulatory constraints we should be aware of (data residency eu/gdpr)?
[11:05] Samir: our customers in eu want logs to remain in europe and we have some defense customers with stricter controls.
[11:12] Riley: we support region pinning for hosted in specific cloud regions and private gives full control; we'll note that for the proposal.
[11:20] Alyssa: what's typical time to spin up a dedicated pool?
[11:24] Riley: depends on quota and availability - a couple days to a couple weeks for reserved capacity provisioning; private on-prem can take longer due to ops.
[11:33] Priya: are there any known model regressions or quality differences when quantizing that we should be aware of?
[11:39] Riley: occasionally quantization can affect math/rare token generation; we recommend running your domain evals. Redwood Optimize flags regressions and suggests alternate kv/quant profiles.
[11:52] Diego: we want example infra diagrams - can you provide an arch doc showing hosted, dedicated, and private flows?
[11:57] Jordan: yes we'll attach an architecture deck and a sample network diagram.
[12:02] Alyssa: okay, last part - decision criteria. our scorecard has: security 30%, latency 25%, cost 20%, multilingual quality 15%, ease of integration 10%.
[12:14] Jordan: that's helpful; we'll tailor the pilot to those metrics.
[12:19] Priya: timeline again - security sign-off by 12/20, benchmark results by 12/23, pilot kickoff early jan.
[12:26] Jordan: great. quick recap of action items...
[12:30] Jordan: 1) we'll send pricing + security whitepaper + architecture diagrams (Jordan) by 12/16. 2) riley will schedule the benchmark run once diego shares sample prompts (riley) by 12/18. 3) alyssa/diego will provide prompt set + RPS profile by 12/17. 4) follow-up call week of 12/22.
[12:53] Alyssa: thanks everyone - appreciate it.
[12:55] Diego: thanks.
[12:56] [END]
